newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists squabble over policy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists squabble over policy.

text.p: French opposition Socialists and Communists squabbled on Monday over who would set policy if the left won a parliamentary election after opinion polls showed the ruling centre-right had rebuilt a clear lead.

Left-wing wrangling was music to the ears of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who has portrayed the French Communists as Cold War dinosaurs unfit to run a modern economy or address problems like France's record 12.8 percent unemployment.

Communist leader Robert Hue, writing in the party daily L'Humanite, said he would demand a say in the policy of any Socialist-led coalition if the left won the May 25-June 1 National Assembly election.
"There will be no left-wing majority without all components of the left -- including the Communist party," Hue wrote in the daily, which has a hammer-and-sickle emblem on its front page.
"And, for this new majority to be formed, all components will have to decide the new policy together."
Hue's line flatly contradicted Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who has insisted that junior partners in a Socialist-led coalition would have to accept Socialist ideas.
Trying to play down the rifts, Jospin said: "There are differences between us but what we share is much greater than what separates us over the different options."
Jospin said in an interview with the Sud-Ouest daily that the Socialists' true opponent was "the ultra-liberal policies that the right would impose if it won power."

Both the Socialists and Communists accuse President Jacques Chirac and Juppe of planning a new bout of austerity to help France qualify for a single European currrency if the centre-right wins the election.
But they disagree on many other issues, especially Europe.

The last two opinion polls showed the centre-right again regaining a lead after the race narrowed to neck-and-neck last week. French bonds and stock prices rallied on the polls -- the CAC-40 stock index was up 1.3 percent in early afternoon.
The latest survey, for the daily Le Figaro, showed the ruling RPR-UDF coalition winning 338 to 370 of the 555 National Assembly seats in mainland France.
The Socialists and their allies were seen trailing on 162-185 with the Communists on 21-28. The far-right National Front was forecast to win up to three.
On European policy, Jospin favours the euro common currency, on several conditions.
Hue opposes the Maastricht Treaty and has called for a referendum on the euro. French voters narrowly approved the treaty in a 1992 referendum.
Jospin wants to create 700,000 jobs, Hue 1.5 million.

Hue and Jospin agree on cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay, but Hue wants it done immediately. The Communists are also planning an increase of 1,000 francs ($175) a month for people earning less than 15,000 francs ($265) a month.

Juppe on Monday accused the left of lacking a clear programme for the economy. "It is extremely surprising that, on such important subjects (as the economy)...that our adversaries should be in such a state of flux," he told a news conference.

Juppe, shown by opinion polls to be deeply unpoplar, said his "absolute priority" was to lower taxes and charges, continue welfare reforms and improve the climate for small businesses. He reiterated calls for the campaign to focus on issues rather than personalities.
He ruled out a face-to-face televised duel with Jospin, who was beaten to the presidency by Chirac in 1995. Juppe wants any duel to include Hue, something Jospin refuses.
Juppe has said Communists in government would cause a crisis for Europe. Jospin noted the late presidents Charles de Gaulle and Francois Mitterrand had named Communist ministers.

Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose National Front has been largely sidelined by the Juppe-Jospin confrontation, said corrupt French politicians deserved to be hanged as some had been under the monarchy before the 1789 Revolution.
